q: What best describes accountable leadership?
options: Holding the highest position on the project organization chart and approving all of the team's work
Being responsible for and taking ownership of the project's objectives, actions and decisions
Assigning blame quickly when something goes wrong
Making every decision alone to keep control
explanation: Accountable leadership is about being responsible and taking ownership of the project's target objectives, the actions taken and the decisions made.

q: What is the difference between authority and leadership?
options: There is no difference
Leadership is granted by the organization; authority is earned by example
Leadership applies only to project managers; authority applies to everyone
Authority is a position of control given by the organization; leadership is inspiring and motivating others by example
explanation: Authority is the position of control given to individuals within the organization. Leadership is about inspiring and motivating others through leading by example.

q: During a workshop, a junior analyst takes the lead in guiding the group to a solution because she knows the topic best. How should this be viewed?
options: As shared leadership, which is typical of high-performing projects
As a breach of the project manager's authority
As scope creep
As a governance failure that should be escalated to the sponsor at once
explanation: Leadership is not exclusive to any role. At different moments a team member or stakeholder may lead, and high-performing projects feature many people exercising leadership.

q: A leader who is open to feedback, works for the team, supports their needs and removes barriers is demonstrating the basis of:
options: Autocratic leadership
Laissez-faire leadership
Servant leadership
Transactional leadership
explanation: Respectfulness, humility and availability, working for the team and removing barriers, form the basis of servant leadership.

q: Two vendor teams on a large project are in conflict over shift rotations. Which response best reflects the Be an Accountable Leader principle?
options: Enforce the contract terms strictly and leave each vendor to deal with its own staff
Bring the vendors together to find the root cause and agree on workable adjustments
Replace one of the vendors immediately
Ignore the conflict, because it is between vendors
explanation: The book contrasts enforcing contracts with holding cross-vendor discussions to explore the root cause and find acceptable adjustments, which resolves the conflict and protects quality and productivity.

q: Team members feel free to raise concerns, ask questions and admit mistakes without fear of punishment. The leader has created:
options: Gold plating
A balanced matrix
A project governance board
Psychological safety
explanation: Leaders foster an environment of psychological safety, where people can speak up without fear.

q: How does the PMBOK Guide, Eighth Edition, describe sustainability?
options: Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Keeping the project within its budget until closing
Maintaining the same team for the entire project
Making sure the product never needs maintenance
explanation: This is the definition used for the principle Integrate Sustainability Within All Project Areas.

q: According to the sustainability pyramid, which response to a negative impact is MOST desirable?
options: Compensate elsewhere for the negative outcome
Restore the impact afterwards
Avoid the negative outcome altogether
Minimize the negative outcome
explanation: From most to least desirable: avoid, minimize, restore, compensate/offset.

q: A project cannot prevent some noise disturbance to a neighborhood, so it pays residents a fee. Where does this sit on the sustainability pyramid?
options: At the very top, as the most desirable response
At the bottom, as the least desirable response
In the middle, equal to minimizing
It is not part of the pyramid
explanation: Compensating or offsetting is the base of the pyramid: acceptable as a minimum, but less desirable than restoring, minimizing or avoiding.

q: The triple bottom line balances which three things?
options: Scope, schedule and cost
Inputs, tools and outputs
Organizational strategy, programs, projects and day-to-day operations
Social equity, environmental stewardship and economic prosperity
explanation: The triple bottom line is people, planet and profit: social, environmental and economic.

q: Who is accountable for integrating sustainability into a project?
options: Project managers, teams and sponsors jointly
Only the sponsor
Only a sustainability officer outside the project
Only the regulators
explanation: Project managers, teams and sponsors are all jointly accountable for integrating sustainability across all project areas and phases.

q: Sustainability goals were not included in the business case. What should the project manager do?
options: Ignore sustainability, because it is out of scope
Add sustainability deliverables without telling the sponsor
Still encourage discussion of sustainability impacts with stakeholders
Stop the project until the business case is rewritten to include sustainability
explanation: Goals should be in formal documents and confirmed by the sponsor. If they are not, the project manager should still encourage discussions about their impact.

q: Which is a recognized challenge of integrating sustainability into projects?
options: It removes the need for stakeholder engagement
It broadens the time horizon and number of stakeholders, which can add cost and complexity
It always reduces project quality
It makes the business case unnecessary
explanation: Sustainability broadens project management to longer time orientations and more stakeholders, which may increase cost or complexity. There are also no universal success criteria.

q: What are team agreements?
options: Contracts between the organization and its suppliers
Rules written by the sponsor and imposed on the team
The legal terms and conditions written into each team member's employment contract
Behavioral parameters and working norms established by the project team itself
explanation: Team agreements are behavioral parameters and working norms established by the project team and upheld through individual and team commitments.

q: When should team agreements be created?
options: At the beginning of the project
Only after the first serious conflict
During project closing
Whenever the sponsor requests them
explanation: They should be created at the beginning of a project to set the norms and practices for ongoing collaboration.

q: Which conditions does an empowered project culture depend on?
options: Strict hierarchy and minimal communication
Team members competing against each other for rewards
Mutual trust and full clarity on roles, responsibilities, team agreements and processes
Keeping stakeholders away from the team
explanation: The environment should promote mutual trust among stakeholders and team members, with full clarity on roles, responsibilities, team agreements and guiding processes.

q: A deliverable is late. In the status meeting the project manager says: "I agreed to that date and I missed a dependency. Here is how I will recover it." Which behavior is she showing?
options: Using her authority to control the team
Accountable leadership: owning her decisions and actions
Shared leadership: letting someone else on the team take the lead for a while
Compensating for a negative outcome
explanation: Accountable leadership means being responsible for, and taking ownership of, the project's objectives, the actions taken and the decisions made. When you accept a piece of work, you are accountable for carrying it out.

q: A project manager notices that when she is under pressure she becomes impatient and dismisses ideas. She starts asking a colleague to chair the tense meetings. Which characteristic of an accountable leader is this?
options: Self-awareness of her own motives
Shared authority
Systems thinking
Stewardship of resources
explanation: Self-awareness is understanding your own motives, values, feelings and strengths, and how they drive your actions. Acting on that understanding is part of leading accountably.

q: A pipeline project has to clear a strip of woodland. After construction it replants the strip with native trees. Which level of the sustainability pyramid is this?
options: Avoid
Minimize
Restore
Compensate
explanation: The pyramid ranks responses to a negative impact: avoid, minimize, restore, compensate. Replanting repairs the impact after it happened, which is restoring. Avoiding would have been routing around the woodland.

q: A company's sustainability strategy requires recycled packaging on everything it ships. A project launching a new product must follow it. How does the strategy reach the project?
options: As a team agreement written and signed by the members of the project team
As a risk response chosen by the project manager
As a lesson learned from an earlier project
As an enterprise environmental factor that imposes requirements
explanation: Organizational sustainability strategies may already apply as EEFs that impose requirements on the project. The team does not control them and must work within them.

q: A construction team can buy the cheapest materials, or slightly dearer ones with far less environmental impact. Applying the sustainability principle, what should it do?
options: Choose the cheapest, because keeping cost down is the project manager's only real duty
Choose the lower-impact sources while still watching value and return
Choose the dearest materials, whatever they cost the project
Leave the choice to the supplier, who knows the materials best
explanation: The principle does not ignore value and return. It asks the team to plan materials carefully, pick sources with the least environmental impact, and involve the local community.

q: A virtual team across four time zones keeps arguing about how fast messages must be answered. The project manager drafts a set of rules alone and emails them to everyone. What would fit an empowered culture better?
options: Letting the team itself set its working norms as team agreements
Asking the sponsor to issue the rules formally, to give them more weight with the team
Removing the team members who answer messages slowly
Waiting for the argument to settle without any intervention
explanation: Team agreements are behavioral parameters and working norms set by the team, upheld by individual and team commitment. Remote and virtual teams face extra difficulty, which makes this more important.

q: A test fails two days before a milestone payment. The sponsor hints that the report could wait until after the payment. The project manager reports the failure on the day it happens. Which characteristic of an accountable leader is this?
options: Shared leadership within the project team
Flexibility and adaptability
Integrity, honesty and fairness
Availability
explanation: An accountable leader's decisions follow moral principles, especially in hard situations, and aim at the common good. That is integrity, honesty and fairness, and it builds trust.

q: A project manager gives close, step-by-step direction to a new team during an outage. With her experienced team, on routine work, she mostly asks questions and lets them decide. Her values are the same with both. Which characteristic is this?
options: Flexibility and adaptability
Self-awareness
Authority
Humility
explanation: Flexibility and adaptability means adapting the leadership style to the situation and the audience without losing core values.

q: A director asks why a project needs more leadership than the department's routine work, which runs smoothly with little of it. What reason does the PMBOK Guide give?
options: Projects have larger budgets than operations do
Project managers have more authority than line managers
Routine work needs no leadership of any kind, because its procedures are fixed in advance
Projects join groups that do not normally work together, with higher stakes
explanation: Projects bring together organizations, departments and vendors that do not normally work together, the stakes are higher, and many people try to influence the outcome. That creates confusion and conflict, so more leadership is needed.

q: A demolition project cannot avoid raising dust near a school. It installs water sprays and screens, and works only outside school hours, so that far less dust reaches the school. Which level of the sustainability pyramid is this?
options: Avoid
Minimize
Restore
Compensate
explanation: The pyramid ranks responses to a negative impact: avoid it altogether, minimize it, restore the impact, or compensate for it. Reducing the dust that cannot be avoided is minimizing.

q: A project manager wants a supplier to be bound to a sustainability target, not merely encouraged to meet it. According to the Guide, where can a sustainability KPI be written so that it applies to the supplier?
options: Only in the lessons learned register
In the team's working agreements
In the contract
Nowhere: such targets cannot be formal
explanation: Sustainability KPIs can be written into the charter, the business case, the scope statement or contracts. A contract is the document that binds a supplier.

q: After a project switches to recycled materials and cuts its energy use, its material and energy bills fall, and a sustainable-finance fund shows interest in the company. Which kind of sustainability benefit is this?
options: Financial
Operational
Organizational
Customer and stakeholder
explanation: Financial benefits include lower material and energy costs, less waste and interest from sustainable-finance investors. Operational benefits are process innovation and less operational waste.

q: A team sees that a weekly reporting activity no longer serves anyone and proposes to stop it. The manager wonders whether a team may propose such a thing. What does the Build an Empowered Culture principle say?
options: No: only the sponsor may question an activity
No: the team's task is to carry out the plan exactly as it was written at the start
Yes, but only after the project has closed
Yes: empowered teams can propose speeding up, slowing or stopping activities
explanation: Empowered teams affect every domain. They can propose speeding up, slowing down or stopping activities, help cut unplanned spending, help define risk thresholds and shape how stakeholders are engaged.

q: Match each one-line summary with the principle of the Eighth Edition it describes.
left: See the project as a connected system
Build it in: prevent, improve, cut waste
Own decisions and outcomes; lead by example
Outcomes and benefits matter more than outputs
right: Embed Quality Into Processes and Deliverables
explanation: Each principle has a short essence: a connected system (holistic view), building it in (quality), owning decisions (accountable leader), trust and team agreements (empowered culture), and outcomes over outputs (value).
